source_text: ἐπεὶ καὶ Παῦλος ἐν ταῖς ἐπιστολαῖς οὐ φιλοσοφίαν διαβάλλων φαίνεται, τὸν δὲ τοῦ γνωστικοῦ μεταλαμβάνοντα ὕψους οὐκέτι παλινδρομεῖν ἀξιοῖ ἐπὶ τὴν Ἑλληνικὴν φιλοσοφίαν, στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου ταύτην ἀλληγορῶν, στοιχειωτικήν τινα οὖσαν καὶ προπαιδείαν τῆς ἀληθείας. διὸ καὶ τοῖς Ἑβραίοις γράφων τοῖς ἐπανακάμπτουσιν εἰς νόμον ἐκ πίστεως ἢ πάλιν φησὶ χρείαν ἔχετε τοῦ διδάσκειν ὑμᾶς, τίνα τὰ στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς τῶν λογίων τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ γεγόνατε χρείαν ἔχοντες γάλακτος καὶ οὐ στερεᾶς τροφῆς. ὡσαύτως ἄρα καὶ τοῖς ἐξ Ἑλλήνων ἐπιστρέφουσι Κολοσσαεῦσι· βλέπετε μή τις ὑμᾶς ἔσται ὁ συλαγωγῶν διὰ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καὶ κενῆς ἀπάτης κατὰ τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν ἀνθρώπων, κατὰ τὰ στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου τούτου καὶ οὐ κατὰ Χριστόν, δελεάζων αὖθις εἰς φιλοσοφίαν ἀναδραμεῖν, τὴν στοιχειώδη διδασκαλίαν. κἂν λέγῃ τις κατὰ σύνεσιν ἀνθρώπων φιλοσοφίαν ηὑρῆσθαι πρὸς Ἑλλήνων, ἀλλὰ τὰς γραφὰς εὑρίσκω τὴν σύνεσιν θεόπεμπτον εἶναι λεγούσας. ὁ γοῦν ψαλμῳδὸς μεγίστην ἡγεῖται δωρεὰν τὴν σύνεσιν καὶ αἰτεῖ λέγων· δοῦλος σός εἰμι ἐγώ· συνέτισόν με. καὶ μή τι τὸ πολύπειρον τῆς γνώσεως αἰτούμενος ὁ Δαβὶδ γράφει· χρηστότητα καὶ παιδείαν καὶ γνῶσιν δίδαξόν με, ὅτι ταῖς ἐντολαῖς σου ἐπίστευσα. κυρίας δ’ εἶναι τὰς διαθήκας ὡμολόγηται καὶ τοῖς τιμιωτέροις δίδοσθαι. λέγει γοῦν ὁ ψαλμὸς πάλιν ἐπὶ τοῦ θεοῦ· οὐκ ἐποίησεν οὕτως οὐδενὶ ἔθνει, καὶ τὰ κρίματα αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἐδήλωσεν αὐτοῖς. τὸ δὲ οὐκ ἐποίησεν οὕτως πεποιηκέναι μὲν δηλοῖ, ἀλλ’ οὐχ οὕτως. ἐν συγκρίσει γοῦν τὸ οὕτως πρὸς τὴν ὑπεροχὴν τὴν καθ’ ἡμᾶς γινομένην· ἐξῆν δὲ δήπου τῷ προφήτῃ εἰπεῖν ἁπλῶς τὸ οὐκ ἐποίησεν ἄνευ τῆς προσθήκης τοῦ οὕτως. ναὶ μὴν καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἐν ταῖς Πράξεσιν ἐπ’ ἀληθείας καταλαμβάνομαι φησίν, ὅτι προσωπολήπτης οὐκ ἔστιν ὁ θεός, ἀλλ’ ἐν παντὶ ἔθνει ὁ φοβούμενος αὐτὸν καὶ ἐργαζόμενος δικαιοσύνην δεκτὸς αὐτῷ ἐστιν.
pass_a_gloss: Since also Paul in the letters appears not to be slandering philosophy, but the one partaking of the height of the gnosis-worthy one is not considered worthy to turn back again to the Greek philosophy, allegorizing the elements of the world, this being a sort of elementary and preparatory education of the truth. Therefore, also writing to the Hebrews who are turning back to the law from faith, or again, he says you have need of someone to teach you what the elements of the beginning of the oracles of God are, and you have come to have need of milk and not solid food. Similarly, then, also to the Colossians who are turning from among the Greeks; beware lest someone will be the one deceiving you through philosophy and empty deceit according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of this world and not according to Christ, enticing again to run back to the elementary teaching. And even if someone should say that philosophy was found according to human understanding among the Greeks, but I find the scriptures saying that understanding is sent by God. For the psalmist indeed considers the greatest gift to be understanding and asks saying: I am your servant; give me understanding. And not asking for the much-experienced thing of knowledge, David writes: teach me goodness and discipline and knowledge, for I have trusted in your commandments. And he acknowledges the covenants to be lordly and to be given to the more honorable ones. For the psalm says again concerning God: he did not do thus to any nation, and his judgments he did not declare to them. But the 'he did not do thus' shows that he did do, but not thus; for in comparison, the 'thus' is with respect to the superiority that is happening among us; but it was possible for the prophet to say simply 'he did not do' without the addition of 'thus'. Yes, indeed, also Peter in the Acts, being taken hold of by the truth, says that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation the one fearing him and working righteousness is acceptable to him.

pass_b_english: Paul does not appear in his letters to be attacking philosophy as such. Rather, he insists that anyone who has shared in the height of true gnosis should never turn back to Greek philosophy. He treats that philosophy as the "elements of the world" — an elementary, preparatory stage for the truth. That is why, when writing to the Hebrews who were drifting back to the law from faith, he tells them they need someone to teach them all over again the first principles of God's oracles; they have become infants who need milk instead of solid food (Heb 5:12).

He makes the same point to the Colossians, who were turning from paganism: "See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of this world and not according to Christ" (Col 2:8), luring you back into that elementary teaching. Even if someone claims that philosophy was discovered by human reason among the Greeks, I find the Scriptures declaring that true understanding is a gift sent by God. The psalmist calls understanding the greatest gift and prays, "I am your servant; give me understanding" (Ps 119:125). David does not ask for mere breadth of knowledge; he writes, "Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, for I have trusted in your commandments" (Ps 119:66).

It is acknowledged that the covenants belong to the Lord and are given to the more honorable. The psalm says of God, "He has not dealt thus with any nation, and He has not made His judgments known to them" (Ps 147:20). The phrase "He has not dealt thus" implies that He has dealt, but not in that way; the "thus" points by comparison to the surpassing privilege now given to us. The prophet could have simply said "He has not dealt" without adding "thus," but he chose the comparative form precisely to highlight this distinction. So too Peter, seized by the truth in Acts, declares, "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears Him and does what is right is acceptable to Him" (Acts 10:34-35).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, particularly the subtle distinction in the discussion of the Psalmist's use of 'οὐκ ἐποίησεν οὕτως' (he did not do thus). Pass A provides a literal rendering, while Pass B provides a fluent English version that correctly incorporates the necessary scripture citations (Heb 5:12, Col 2:8, Ps 119:125, Ps 119:66, Ps 147:20, Acts 10:34-35) which correspond to the Greek content and allusions.
